speechtext: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 30, to amend the Admiralty Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the law the
Exchequer court in Canada is a court of admiralty and as suc'h has within Canada all the jurisdiction, powers and authority conferred by the Admiralty Act of 1890. The Privy Council in recent cases has decided that this should not apply to the changes which have been made giving additional powers to the High Court of Admiralty since 1890. This bill is to give to the Admiralty court all the powers which courts of the same class have in England.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 31, to amend the Supreme Court Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
By this bill the spring
sittings of the court, which, as the law stands at the present time, are fixed for the first Tuesday in May, will be advanced to the

Dominion Elections Act

fourth Tuesday in April. This is done because it will be more convenient for the judges and, I believe, also for the lawyers.
There is another somewhat important amendment by which it is intended to confer upon the court discretionary power in special cases to receive evidence in addition to that which is embodied in the stated case. The Privy Council in England and the High Court of Appeal in England have such powers and it has happened in a Canadian case that the supreme court here had no authority or discretion to allow the filing of a plan while, When the case was before the Privy Council, the Privy Council allowed the filing of that plan. Mr. L. P. BANCROFT (Selkirk) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 32, to amend the Dominion Elections Act (voting by clergymen, teachers and students).
Explain.

This bill seeks to amend paragraph (c) of section 29 of the Dominion Elections Act, which reads as follows:
(c) Who has ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election.
As the election writs are usually issued about two months before election day, the present act disfranchises all persons Who change their places of residence dluring four months immediately preceding the date of an election. Clergymen changing pastorates usually do so during July or August, school teachers begin their duties about September 1, and students in the higher institutions about October 1. Every federal election since 1896 has been held during the fall months. All clergymen, teachers and students, who in following their respective duties, change their place of residence within four months preceding the date of an election are disfranchised under the present act.
This amendment exempts clergymen, teachers and students from paragraph (c) of section 29, provided that they can satisfy the registrar that they are othewise qualified to have their names placed on the voters' list. This amendment affects approximately 12,000 clergymen, 63,000 teachers and 75,000 students.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Patent Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-manufacture for reasonable requirements.

What change does this
make in the existing law?

As I explained somewhat briefly on the first reading, the purpose of this amendment is to bring the Patent Act into conformity with the terms of the international convention for the protection of industrial property, which was agreed to at The Hague conference in 1925. Canada was represented at that conference by Mr. Frederick Herbert Palmer, Canadian government trade commissioner, and we were a party to the convention, which was signed on our behalf by our representative. The intention now is to incorporate in the Patent Act the changes which were agreed upon at The Hague conference.
Hon. members will notice that the changes that are being made are underlined in the bill before them. It has always been the law that every patentee must satisfy the reasonable requirements of the public with reference to his patent. It was thought by The Hague conference that this provision might be made clearer, and that every country that was a party to the convention should agree not only that [the patented article should meet the requirements of the public, but that it should be manufactured in the country. That is the reason, Mr. Chairman, for the amendments that are proposed to subsections (b) and (c) of section 40 of the act. Subsection (b) as proposed to be amended will read:
Patent Act [DOT]

Any person interested may present a petition to the commissioner alleging that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to a patented invention have not been satisfied-
Then follows the addition:

or that the patentee has failed to adequately manufacture the patented invention in Canada.
and so forth.

What is the minister's
definition of "reasonable requirements" of the public? How does he arrive at his definition?

I believe that the very
reason why this change is proposed is that there was confusion as to just what was meant by that phrase. It has often been the experience of the department, and I believe of similar departments in other countries, that after an article has been patented, the patent simply lies there in oblivion without any attempt being made, at all to give the public the benefit of the invention. I would interpret the words "reasonable requirements of the public" to mean that the public could reasonably buy the patented article, and that it should be on the market in sufficient numbers to be available to any purchaser. I believe the reason for the change in the section which is now embodied in the bill amending the original act is to make the act clear, not only that the patentee is required to see that the requirements of the public are looked after, but to see that the patented article is manufactured in the country.
Does that mean that he will lose his right if he does not manufacture the article?

No. There is provision
made in reigard to that. We will come to it in another section. If the requirements of the public are not satisfied, or if the patentee fails to manufacture the article, any citizen may apply for a license to manufacture the article.
That is terrible.
That has been the law for a long while.
It robs a man of his right.

Referring to paragraph (b), it is provided that the patentee be ordered to supply the patented article at a reasonable price. I would ask the minister whether 'he has any organization in his department which can determine whether a patented article is sold at a reasonable price or not.

It is pretty hard to determine what is a reasonable price. I suppose there is competition. I suppose a reasonable price is arrived at having reference to the prices of similar articles. In the case of a patented article which would be in a class by itself I would interpret this section as being within the discretion of the department to determine, whether the price is reasonable or not, but I may say there is no intention on the part of the department to fix the price of the article. The only discretion is to determine whether the patented article is sold at a reasonable price, and if not the department would have authority to grant a license to someone else, in order to place a similar article at the disposal of the public at -a lower price. I think that is what it would mean.
Section 40 subsection (c) provides for that very thing-that the commissioner may fix the price.

I would 'call the attention of the minister to the glaring defect in the drafting of the section which I know as a literary man he will appreciate. The draftsman has employed the practice of splitting the infinitive. At the end of the nineteenth line I find the words:	,
Or that the patentee has failed to adequately manufacture.
If it were made to read "has failed to manufacture adequately," I think it would be more in harmony with literary taste and good English.

If my hon. friend the minister will look at paragraph (c) of section 40 he will observe on the second page of the bill the provision that the order shall not be made less than one year after the thirteenth day of June 1023. All those words are wholly unnecessary in 1928, because he is merely reenacting a section which has been repealed. To speak of 1923 at this time in 1928 would obviously have no application at all and might as well be deleted from the bill.

I would ask my hon.
friend to make that point clear to me.

The statute apparently
was passed prior to 1923, and provision is made that no order shall be issued before the expiration of three years from the date of the patent and "not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three". Obviously any order that can be made in 1928 must be at least one year after the 13th day of June, 1923. Those words can have no possible application.

Patent Act

It saye "not more tlhan
one year after the passing of the act".

That was originally
intended, but you have substituted the words, "not less than one year after the thirteenth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three". This is five years later.

from?

There is a mistake
somewhere, because my copy does not read the same as my hon. friend's. I do not know whether the mistake has been made by the law officers or not. I think we had better let the section stand. I observe that the bills that have been placed at the disposal of the members are different from the one I have. My copy reads:
Provided that such an order shall not be made before the expiration of three years from the date of the patent, and not less than one year after the passing of this act.
That is perfectly clear.
I never intended anything different from that, so that I would like to amend the bill.

I think you had better
let the section stand, so as to have no doubt about it, and make the amendment in the meantime.

That section has the

That is a mistake in the

speechtext: Is this the form of agreement that is generally entered into between two railway companies under such circumstances?

subtopic: ROSEDALE-BULLPOTJND BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
I do not think it would be correct to say that this is the general form of agreement. I do not know that any such general form exists; the form depends upon the peculiar circumstances of the case. As my hon. friend knows, both railway companies in 1924 desired to construct'a line through the territory covered by what is now known as the Rosedale-Bullpound branch line, and the railway committee of this house decided that it was in the interests of Canada to have the railway companies get together on a joint section through that district. From 1924 until now the two companies have been endeavouring to agree to the precise terms of a contract between them covering the

construction and operation of that joint section. These terms have now been hammered out to the satisfaction of both companies, and the department has reviewed the matter in so far as it may be said to affect the general interests of the public. speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
This bill, like many others now
on the order paper, purports to amend a chapter of the revised statutes of Canada. These statutes came into force on the 1st day of February of this year, and virtually before they have become effective legislation is actually prepared to amend them. This is a very great waste of public money; moreover, it is a considerable inconvenience not only to judges and to the legal profession blit also to the community generally. I took up five bills the other day, one after the other, each of which proposes a trifling amendment to a statute that came into force on the 1st day of February of this year. I submit that the government, with a little care, might have provided against that contingency because it is not only, as I say, inconvenient, but expensive to the public that this necessity should arise.

I agree with my hon.
friend; his point is well taken as regards such amendments as we may be tempted to submit to the house as a matter of general practice. However, I plead in favour of this bill that it is in the same predicament as a previous one which I presented to the house for second reading this afternoon. The intention is to bring our statutes into conformity with decisions arrived at by an international congress at which we were represented.
That was in 1925, as my hon. friend will remember.

I quite agree that it
would have been desirable to have had these amendments agreed upon last year, but as my hon. friend knows, last session was very

Trade Mark and Design Act
brief and it was not possible to attain all the results which we might have aimed at had parliament sat longer. When we prorogued in April these changes were hardly in form for presentation to the house.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to authorize an extension of time for the completion of the St. John and Quebec Railway between Centre-ville, in the county of Carleton, and Andover, in the county of Victoria, N.B.
Explain.
When the bill was introduced I made an explanation. If we go into committee now I shall be glad to deal with any phase of the matter.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Extension of time.

As I stated when the
bill was first introduced, the St. John and Quebec Railway Company is owned by the province of New Brunswick, the government of -which province has requested an extension of time for the completion of this branch. The section now before the house is designed to give the Minister of Railways power to grant that extension.

My sole reason for
directing attention to the bill is that in my opinion the company became dead on the first day of December 1927. The time within which the minister might extend the period for construction expired on December 1 last, and inasmuch as it expired on that day there ceased to be a company. So I suggest that additional sections should be added to the bill to make it clear beyond doubt that the corporation as such still exists, because by virtue of the extension having expired before legislation was introduced, the company is no longer existent.

That point naturally
arose in giving consideration to the matter, and I adopted the obvious course for a poor layman; I referred it to the legal department of the government, the Department of Justice, and it is on the advice of the Department of Justice that the bill is presented in its present

St. John and Quebec Railway
form. I am sorry I cannot discuss the legal niceties of the situation with my hon. friend, but apparently the Department of Justice is satisfied that this will effect the purpose desired.
I have no desire to enter into any legal discussion, but after the first day of December last there was no longer a company.
I doubt that.

If my hon. friend will
take the trouble to look at the statutes of 1925 he will find that the power of the minister was extended until December 1, 1927, and when that date was passed there was no longer any right to construct a railway, and with the right to construct the railway the corporate powers of the company vanished, partially at least. It is a matter on which the Department of Justice can more readily advise than I can, but we are now giving that power until 1930, although the company as such suffered the legal result following the expiration of the period of time allowed.
Does my hon. friend say that the company has gone out of existence?
I said partially.

I would point out that
this company is in existence as the owner of Certain railway lines in the province of New Brunswick which are leased and operated by the Canadian National Railways. Therefore the company must of necessity continue to exist; it could not have become defunct on December 1 of last year. The point with respect to that, as I understand it, was that the power of the minister to extend the time expired on that date. That point was referred to the Department of Justice, who have advised me that if it is dealt with in this manner it will be satisfactory and will effect the purpose desired. Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Experimental Farms Stations Act.
_ Mr. BENNETT:	There is a principle
involved in this bill, Mr. Speaker. Parliament created these establishments and provided that parliament itself should determine what areas should thereafter be acquired and* what moneys should be 
expended. This amendment substitutes the governor in council, on the report of the minister, and while one need not have any lack of confidence with respect to the present incumbent of that office I think it desirable, where it is possible, that we should not extend the powers of the governor in council beyond what has heretofore been the case, when parliament may reasonably exercise the power without any inconvenience. I would point out that preceding governments have been acquiring other farms for the last thirty or forty years without any authority whatever. The original bill prescribed the acreage limitation of the first five farms, but that has been entirely disregarded ever since. Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 11, to amend the Seeds Act.
M*r. G. G. COOTE (Macleod): May I ask the minister if it is proposed to send this bill to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

I did explain it on the first reading, but I will do so again. There are two main amendments proposed, the first having to do with the rearranging of the names. This has been threshed out by the seed growers of the west on several occasions, and the names and grades of the various registered seeds are rearranged as shown on page 2 of the bill. In regard to the other amendment, two years ago parliament authorized the minister to license new varieties of seed grain. That matter of licensing has been somewhat abused. The minister has no authority to refuse a license when the variety is not a sound one; for

Royal Military College
instance, a license has to be granted regardless of the quality of the grain. Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence) moved the second reading of Bill No. 13, respecting the Royal Military College of Canada.
Will the minister explain what he proposes in this bill? I have had correspondence from various people about it.

This bill is intended to
bring up to date the provisions of the act respecting the Royal Military College. As a matter of fact, the provisions which were in the revised statutes of 1906 and which have been continued until the present time, have not been in accordance with the practice which has been adopted in the department since 1910 or 1911. I refer particularly to the matter of qualifications for admission, which, under the old act, are passed on by boards in the provinces and which, by'regulation and practice, have been passed upon by a central board, depending upon the_ certificates held by applicants from educational institutions in the provinces. With regard to the number of students the act provides a limitation of 120, which has been exceeded practically every year since 1913 with the exception, I think, of two. The provision
limiting the pay of the staff was exceeded as far back as 1913. This bill is intended, as the explanatory notes show, to remove those limitations and to provide for admission under regulations made by the governor in council which will be published in the Canada Gazette.

The real fact of the
matter is that this is a statute to repeal the existing statute, under which parliament has some control and had made certain provisions, and to substitute for it the discretion of the governor in council. In other words, it becomes purely a political control as distinguished from a parliamentary control. I submit that this is a step in the wrong direction, especially with respect to the Royal Military College, an institution which has rendered great service to this country and which has graduated very distinguished men who have brought great credit to Canada both at home and abroad. Whatever may have been the defects of that system, it is certain, with respect to education, that graduates of that institution have taken a foremost place in almost every part of the world in many branches of human endeavour, not solely confined to military achievements. The number of students that could attend this institution was limited by statute, and1 quotas were provided for the various provinces. The control with respect, not to the quota but to the pay and the sum total of the numbers that could attend, was a parliamentary control. Heretofore the quota has been regulated by considerations that were referable to that military provision, and while the payments, the character of the instruction given and the government and control of the institution were, perhaps, under the control of the governor in council, there were in the statute itself details with respect to those matters.
A number of old graduates are tremendously interested in this institution, and some of them feel-and I hope they are wrong-that this endeavour at this time to take the control of it entirely out of parliament and to substitute for it practically a political control, as all control by governor in council is, cannot but be fraught with disaster to the institution. There is a feeling that it would be much better if an effort were -made to create for the institution a body of government _ that would be entirely removed from political control. institution shall be known as The Royal Military College of Canada, and shall be located m some one of the garrison toms of Canada, and shall be under the direction and management of the Minister of National Defence.

Now that was not the original intention when this college was instituted in this country away back about the year 1874. The countiy is proud of this institution. speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
As I
pointed out the other day when this bill was introduced, last year this amendment was passed by the Senate, where it was introduced, and it arrived in this house too late to be considered, chiefly owing to the fact that some interested members from British Columbia were not present when the bill came up for consideration. The purpose of the bill is briefly to suspend section 11 and to repeal section 12 of the act. In British Columbia the federal government control the railway belt and the Peace River block and they have the administration of the natural resources in that territory in British Columbia. The British Columbia legislature passed a water act for the governance of the supplies of water under provincial jurisdiction and the federal government adopted the provincial bill. The water rights in the federal belt were administered by the provincial bill. The water rights in the federal belt were administered by the provincial authorities under the control of a minister of the provincial government. In 1924 they consolidated their act and in 1926 we sought to bring our water rights act into conformity with the British Columbia act. Some difficulties arose when we were bringing our act into conformity with theirs with regard to certain Indian rights under the Indian department, over which I have control, and the question arose as to whether the rights of riparian owners were sufficiently safeguarded. We therefore inserted in our bill, in addition to the sections of the British Columbia bill, sections 11 and 12, which provided that in certain cases specified in section 11, before the actuai confirmation of the license by the provincial authorities could take place there must be consent by the Minister of the Interior. This was very much resented by the department in British Columbia, and for a time there was a complete cessation of the issue of permits, because, they said, the control was wrested from them and retained by the Minister of the Interior. After careful consideration I came to the conclusion that it was not
Railway Belt Water Act

worth while to have this controversy go on because interested parties were suffering in consequence, and I agreed last year to the introduction of a bill, which waS introduced in the Senate, not repealing section 11 in its entirety but suspending its operation until it might be required, when it could be put in force by order in council as set out in the bill.
So far as section 12 is concerned, we have decided that the rights of the riparian owners .are safeguarded by section 4 of the act itself, and that there is no real necessity for its retention.

I am pleased indeed to
hear the explanation of the minister. When his amendments were introduced in 1926 I made some objection, but at the present time what I am interested in is to know if under the present amendments any rights held by the users of water in the railway belt are affected in any shape or form, and also whether under the amendment made in 1926 any rights have been acquired which could not have been acquired without the consent of British Columbia. Those are the two principal points I would like cleared up. I might point out to the minister, as I did when this matter was up before, that you might as well give a man a piece of land on the top of mount Everest as to give him land in the railway belt without water, for without water the land is of no use in many parts of that belt. I should like to be assured, therefore, that the rights of the users of water in the railway belt of British Columbia will not be interfered with.
I was not aware until now that this legislation was the result of a little family quarrel. Apparently the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Lands in the province of British Columbia have had a little jar between themselves. We quite understand our Minister of Lands out in British Columbia, and I am glad to see that the Minister of the Interior has felt a little touch of Mr. Pattullo's temper in connection with this matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER

speechtext:
Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Public Printing and Stationery Act in relation to advances authorized to be made to the king's printer for the purchase of materials, to execute orders and requisitions and payment of wages, and to provide that the total amount of such advances shall at no time exceed the sum of seven hundred thousand dollars or such sum as may hereafter be determined, from time to time, by the governor in council.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext: What is it about?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext: The purpose of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, and of the bill that will follow it, is to provide the king's printer with the working capital necessary to enable him to carry out the responsibility imposed upon him by the statute. As hon. gentlemen are aware, the king's printer has to execute printing of all kinds required by the houses of parliament and by every branch of the service of the government of Canada, and has to provide all stationery and office appliances required by the houses of parliament and the various branches of the service. He has to edit the Canada Gazette, and has to be the distributing agent of the various departments for their respective publications, and to be the exclusive sales agent of all the official publications. He has to audit the accounts for all advertising undertaken on behalf of the departments of the government. Under the terms of the statute the Minister of Finance authorizes advances to the king's printer, and the king's printer remits to the receiver general all moneys received for services rendered by the department. The king's printer necessarily carries an extensive and varied assortment of paper and other printing and binding supplies, estimated to average in value approximately $350,000, and a stock of goods classed generally as stationery and office supplies estimated to average in value approximately $150,000; and that amount increases with the large increase in the work of the different departments.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext: The minister wants $700000?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO THE KING'S PRINTER
speechtext:
The amount required
for printing and binding is $350,000. Funds must be provided, therefore, first for the maintenance of this permanent stock, the details

Printing and Stationery Act
of which are of course continually changing, and also for meeting contingent expenditure arising between the date of service rendered and receipt of payments due on account of same. Section 38 of the statute as it stands provides that the Minister of Finance may authorize the advance to the king's printer of a sum not to exceed 8200,000, but for many years, as far as my information goes, and for last year, as I know personally, having been in charge of the department, the amount advanced to the king's printer has much* exceeded the amount provided by the statute. Two causes have combined to render this sum insufficient properly to meet the king's printer's present necessities. . The first is a very large increase in all branches of the activities of the department and the second is the change in money values, which necessarily has its influence upon the wages of the different employees of the printing bureau and the general expenditure connected with it. Therefore it is proposed by this resolution and the bill which will follow to increase the amount which is provided by the statute from 8200,000 to 8700,000. As I have explained, this is not an expenditure at all; it is merely a readjustment. In past years the auditor general has brought to our attention the fact that we were exceeding the terms of the statute. There was some confusion as to the meaning of it. The statute said that the advance should not at any time exceed 8200,000; I believe the intention of it was very clearly to say that it should not exceed cumulatively that amount, but it was interpreted for the sake of carrying on as if no one advance should exceed $200,000. We find that we cannot carry on the printing work with that rather small amount, and therefore we propose now tc bring the working of the printing bureau into clearer harmony with the spirit of the statute by providing that the Department of Finance will be authorized to make advances to the amount of $700,000. As I have said, to-day we carry a stock in excess of 8500,000, and it is likely to increase with the years to come. So we want to provide for the future, and thus meet the wishes of the leader of the opposition that parliament should not be called upon to amend statutes all the time.
The other part of the resolution providing that from time to time the sum may be determined by the governor in council is to cover this contingency. In 1926, although the session was very much prolonged the estimates could not be voted, and .the printing bureau found it very hard to carry on, even had it been possible to be advanced the amount now provided for by the resolution.
XMr. Rinfret.]
As I have explained, this legislation will not have the effect of increasing our expenditure in the printing bureau; it will merely put an end to the somewhat confused interpretation of the statute that has obtained in the past, and bring its workings into clearer harmony with the spirit of the statute.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF SECTION 198, RESPECTING DLASPHEMOUS LIBEL
speechtext:
This piece of legislation has come down to us from a very early date. It has rarely been used in England and, so far as we can discover, it has been used only once in Canada, namely, last year, when for the first time most people in this country realized that such a law was on the statute books. It was then used in the case of Ernest V. Sterry, of the city of Toronto, who was charged with blasphemy on the ground of his having written an article entitled " The Jewish God In connection with the trial Judge Coatsworth made the following statements which, I think, will give us some idea of the interpretation which may be placed upon this statute:
The Bible, the holy scriptures, are to us the revelation of God's will concerning us and all His people. We look upon the Bible as the basis of every good law in our country.
In the light of some of the recent controversies we might very well ask: Which Bible? Judge Coatsworth continues:
. When a man begins to express his opinions m a way that hurts others then he should be curbed whether his opinions are right or wrong.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that goes too far if we are to have any liberty in the expression of opinion in this country. Judge Coatsworth's interpretation is:
WTien a man begins to express his opinion in a way that hurts others, then he should be curbed whether his opinions are right or wrong.
I may say that after I introduced this bill last year, I received a number of communications endorsing the measure which I proposed, a great many of them coming from clergymen of various denominations' who felt that it was not at all necessary in order to protect religion that this legislation as it now stands should continue on the statute books. Articles of protest were written at the time, and perhaps one of the best was that by a Toronto Jewish rabbi. As the Jewish people were the people who might be supposed to be most offended by the blasphemy, since it was concerning the Jewish god, possibly I may be permitted to read just two or three paragraphs from this defence of Mr. Sterry. Rabbi Isserman refers to the old Jewish idea of blasphemy. Going back to the early days, he states:
Because of this power of names, the ancient Israelite never pronounced the name of God.
That was the beginning of the idea. The name of God itself was so sacred that it

Criminal Code
could not be pronounced, and hence anybody who in any way said anything concerning the God of that day was regarded as a blasphemer. Further than that, there were at that time certain social implications. As this writer says:
Blaspheming his name, which meant besmirching his character, made the deity very angry, and man therefore hastened to punish the offender in order to mollify the righteous anger of God. For the whole tribe would be held to account for one man's unpunished offence against God.
It was out of that atmosphere that the idea in regard to blasphemy evolved. The writer of this article then goes on to trace the gradual evolution of the idea of God. He says:
The God whom men feel desires the death of the blasphemer has been supplanted and displaced in the history of Israel.
Again:
For this narrow and limited idea of God represents a stage in the evolution of religion. It represents an epoch in man's growing and evolving consciousness of God.
Again:
It is incorrect to speak of the God idea of the Bible-for the Bible reveals many concepts about God.
Again:
Organized religion need not fear the attacks of unbelievers. It has capable spokesmen. It has excellent organization. It has public opinion and the press to aid it. It has funds at its disposal. It has printing presses and authors and thinkers who are ready to break lances in its behalf. It will weather all attacks. It may purge itself when necessary, but it will endure and no pious people need fear any one publication or any one group of heretics.
He concludes with these words, which I commend to the house:
And, truly, I do not believe that words blaspheme the Deity-but rather deeds. Injustice is blasphemy. Prejudice is blasphemy. War is blasphemy. Poverty is blasphemy. Persecution is blasphemy. Evil in life and deed, and not in word, is blasphemy. The God of to-day is pained, not by words, but by acts, and as I look on the history of humanity, the greatest blasphemies that I know of were committed by men dedicated to God, who though walking with psalms on their lips and symbols of God in their hands, kindled the faggots which burnt the heretical blasphemers. That was real blasphemy-men dedicated to love burning in the name of God a fellow human created in His image. And from such blasphemy may all of us be protected and saved,
I think, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the spirit of a Jewish rabbi, who might have been expected to have been the most offended by the article in question may very well be emulated by the public at large in regard to a matter of this kind. One of the difficulties with this
legislation as it now stands is that there is no definition of blasphemy. The beliefs of one religious group are undoubtedly blasphemies in the eyes of other groups. I wonder if I may recall to the minds of some members of the house the thirty-nine articles of the Church of England. In the thirty-first article I read this:
Wherefore the sacrifices of Masses, in the which it was commonly said, that the priest did offer Christ for the quick and the dead, to have remission of pain or guilt, were blasphemous fables, and dangerous deceits.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a man ought to be able to hold in this country his opinion with regard to masses without being in danger of being charged before the courts with blasphemy.

I submit, without going into this matter any more fully-perhaps already I have dealt with it further than is necessary-that it is not desirable for us to retain on the statute books a law of this character. As I said previously it has been invoked only once in the history of Canada. It stands, however, as a menace to the free expression of religious opinion. I know there is a safeguarding clause here which says:
Provided that no one is guilty of a blasphemous libel for expressing in good faith and in decent language, or attempting to establish by arguments used in good faith and conveyed in decent language, any opinion whatever upon any religious subject.
The article in question, which I have read carefully, is no more extreme than many articles which are written, in perhaps less popular language, in the theological journals of a great many bodies that are carrying on religious work here in Canada. This man Sterry may have been infelicitous in his way of expressing himself, but I repeat that it is dangerous to leave on the statute books a law which may 'be invoked against an individual for expressing himself along religious lines.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF SECTION 198, RESPECTING DLASPHEMOUS LIBEL
speechtext:
The section which the hon. gentleman wishes to repeal reads as follows:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment who publishes any blasphemous libel.
(2) Whether any particular published matter is a blasphemous libel or not is a question of fact: Provided that no one is guilty of a blasphemous libel for expressing in good faith and in decent language, or attempting to establish by arguments used in good faith and conveyed in decent language, any opinion whatever upon any religious subject.
That section is pretty broad. Perhaps my hon. friend does not realize what would be the effect of this bill if it were adopted into law. Our criminal code is in large part a codification of the common law, but it is specially provided that the common law still exists in respect to cases which are not provided for in the code. The repeal of the section to which my hon. friend has reference would not have the effect of repealing the common law, and under the common law those gentlemen whom my hon. friend desires to protect would be prosecuted more severely than under the code. The provisions of the code are rather a modification of the common law by making it less strict and less severe than it would be if this section were repealed. The house must see by the language of the section that any opinion may be freely expressed on any religious subject provided that nothing is said which would really con-

stitute an outrageous reflection upon the religious feeling of the community. After all, this is the law in most countries. It is the law in England; it is the law in the United States of America, and I do not think we should be so anxious to protect people who really want to offend what is the religious feeling of the people of Canada. This is a Christian country, and with all the freedom of speech we have, of which I am myself an advocate, I do not think that this section m either code has worked any injury. I do not know the circumstances of the case my hon. friend mentions, which seems to have been the cause of the present bill, but if the verdict in that case was strict, as does occasionally happen, that does not mean that the law is necessarily wrong. I understand the case was appealed from the decision of the magistrate to the appellate division of the high court of Ontario, and that the verdict and sentence were affirmed. I Should certainly not be disposed to accept this bill and I will vote against the second reading, because I am opposed to the principle.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF SECTION 198, RESPECTING DLASPHEMOUS LIBEL
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to do so I will now finish what I started to say. This article is a burlesque on the story of creation; true, it is expressed in rather vulgar language, but the house can take it from me that this article expresses the story in a manner not more disrespectful than the language you might hear at any society tea table throughout this country. It is becoming customary to speak of that story with more or less disrespect. This gentleman, whoever he is, has followed the example of his betters; he has undertaken to criticize that story in a manner which, as I have said, makes his article something of a burlesque, but not one bit worse than the discussions of men who are supposed to be more respectable than he is. I could go to almost any theological college in Canada and find professors of Old Testament history who give, during their lectures, an account of the story of creation not one whit more respectable than this article. They might use more polite language, more scholarly and erudite expressions, but it would be no different in meaning. This unfortunate man happily does not belong to the elite; he is apparently some rough-mannered, long-haired individual who jumps on a soap box somewhere in the holy city of Toronto, which stands four-square against the waves of
heterodoxy sweeping over the country, a city hallowed by its staunch support of all that is orthodox and traditional both in fiscal theory and in biblical belief.
A great deal of fuss has been made about nothing; this theory of creation given in this article is commonly held from one end of Canada to the other. It is taught in our . Sunday schools and in our day schools in language which is perhaps a little more correct, yet my hon. friend thinks it terrible, and warns the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself not to read it. I can tell him that I have read it with great gusto. I was also pleasantly surprised to find how sensitive the hon. leader of the opposition is for the traditions and faith of the house; he even interrupted me in the little time I had at my disposal to deal with this matter.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF SECTION 198, RESPECTING DLASPHEMOUS LIBEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make just one observation. The hon. member who brought this bill before the house quoted in support of it articles of certain faiths. I sent out for the standard work on criminal law in Canada, Crankshaw's Criminal Code, and turned up the section in question. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has already read it, but I would like to read just one or two comments which appear under that section. The first of these will be found on page 203
of the 1924 edition:
A blasphemous libel consists in the publication of any profane words vilifying or ridiculing God, Jesus Christ, the Holy Ghost, the Old or New Testament or Christianity in general, with intent to shock and insult believers, or to pervert or mislead the ignorant and unwary; and it a publication be "full of scurrilous and opprobrious language, if sacred subjects are ti eateu with levity, if indiscriminate abuse is employed instead of argument, then a design to wound the religious feelings of others may be readily inferred. But where the work is free from all offensive levity, abuse and sophistry, and, in fact, the honest and temperate expression of religious opinions conscientiously held and avowed, it is not a blasphemous libel.
I pass on merely to read one quotation from a judgment of Lord Coleridge, who was Lord Chief Justice of England, in the case of the King against Ramsay and Foote, in which he said:
If the decencies of controversy are observed, even the fundamentals of religion may be attacked, without a person being guilty of blasphemous libel.
That is the law which this amendment is designed to change.
Motion (Mr. Woodsworth) negatived.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution, Mr. Johnston in the chair:
Resolved, that the Governor in Council be authorized to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act such sum or sums of money as may be required, not to exceed in the whole the sum of five hundred million dollars, for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada and for purchasing and withdrawing from circulation unmatured securities of Canada; the principal and interest to be charged upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: May we have some explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: I gave the explanation before six o'clock.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
There is a very great
deal to be said with respect to this matter, because it is involved in the application of a principle which has been applied on several occasions in Great Britain, but I shall not endeavour to' discuss the matter to-night. I will reserve my criticism and suggestions for the second reading of the bill, without in any sense concurring in the resolution now before the house.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: Just as a matter of information I wish the Minister of Finance would inform the committee how he proposes to borrow money, say next year, at a rate of interest which may range from one per cent to four per cent, to retire bonds paying five and one-half per cent in 1932 or 1933, as the case may be, without losing money? I do not see how it can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
That is quite a reasonable
question, Mr. Chairman, and if we find that at the rates of interest Which are suggested we cannot convert these outstanding bonds, we will not do it. I think the record of the government goes to show that any re-financing has always been done at a low rate of interest, and that will be the policy followed in this case. We are simply asking parliament to give us the authority so that if we find it possible' to convert these outstanding loans at a rate of interest sufficiently low to save the country something on the interest, we will do so. V e are told by financial men from time to time that there are frequent transactions going through their books involving these outstanding bonds, and we are advised that by a refunding arrangement, enabling 
people who hold these outstanding bonds now at a high rate of interest to refund them, we will save money. Let me say now that we will try to provide in future that in loans of this magnitude it will be possible for the Minister of Finance to call in these bonds, if he finds the market so working that it will be to the advantage of the country to do so, and refund them again at a low rate of interest.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
Before six o'clock the
minister gave us various items which were to be refunded in the next few yearn. I believe the first large item was about $446,000,000, due in 1933, and in 1934 we have another large sum of about $511,000,000. The other figures given by the minister ranged from $53,000,000 to $73,000,000, in different issues, and he also made the statement that he expected to pay the smaller bond issues in cash up to 1932. In view of the fact that the real refunding will be in connection with the larger loans, is it within the power of the minister to call in those issues before they mature, and pay them off or refund them? I suppose that would be a question of bargaining, but I would like the minister to explain the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: We have no authority to say to my hon. friend or to any other person holding these bonds, " Bring in your bonds and we will give you cash for them." We believe, however, that we can put a price on them which will be attractive and which will permit us to refund them at a rate of interest which will result in a saving to the country.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: Could the minister give us any idea as to where these bonds are held?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: No, I have no idea where these particular bonds are held, but I can give the house information as to the bonds payable outside of Canada. Between 1929 and 1952 there are payable in New York bonds to the value of about $225,874,000, while there are bonds maturing in London between 1934 and 1960, inclusive, amounting to $311,668,138.39. The debt of the country is largely held in Canada.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: May I ask if any portion of the bonds which the minister contemplates retiring by this loan are tax free bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
That information is not on
record; I have just sent out for it, but there is a considerable proportion of these bonds which are tax free.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
The 1933 bonds are
tax free, while the 1934 bonds are taxable.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Most of them are payable in
Canada; some are payable in New York while some are payable in both Canada and New York. maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext: I believe I can answer the question which was asked by my hon. friend. The 1933 issue is payable in Canada only; it is non-taxable and is apparently the issue which this $500,000,000 is intended to retire. That issue is not payable anywhere except in Canada.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the risk
of making myself appear ridiculous to hon. members of this house who may claim to be high financiers, I desire to offer just one suggestion which I have made to the minister on previous occasions, but which I regret to say he has not as yet seen fit to accept. I do not believe we will have a better opportunity than the present to take over our own bonds. When all is said and done, the bonds which will be issued for this loan of $500 000,000 will be issued against the credit of Canada. I care not if the minister has to go to New York to get the loan, he will have to take Canada in his pocket; he will have to deposit Canada in Wall street and go to the front door to borrow back a portion of Canada at 4 per cent or 5 per cent as the case may be. I am still at a loss to know why that credit, which is good enough for Wall street, is not good enough for Canada, and I still wait for the minister to answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
I do not want to be
discourteous to my friend, but I repeat that
the debt of Canada is largely held by Canadians, and in this refunding operation we propose to give Canadians the preference. But I say to the bond men and to the bankers of Canada that they will have to meet the rates of the world to get the business, or we will go elsewhere.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL BRANCH OFFICES FOR REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES
speechtext:
This resolution states
that it is necessary to create further offices for the redemption of Dominion notes. Would the minister tell us how this work is carried on, how these Dominion notes are redeemed, with what, and so forth?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ADDITIONAL BRANCH OFFICES FOR REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES
speechtext:
The offices of the assistant
receivers general do exactly the same work as the head office in the capital of the country. The functions of these offices are to distribute to the banks Dominion notes and specie, to make advances to them under the provisions of the Finance Act and to act as registrars of notices of intention to give security under section 88 of the Bank Act. They also act as transfer agents in connection with the registration and de-registration of Dominion bonds. Principal and interest of government bonds and certain guaranteed issues of the Canadian National Railways are also payable at these offices.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL BRANCH OFFICES FOR REDEMPTION OF DOMINION NOTES
speechtext:
It was asserted, rightly
or wrongly, that to have more than one office in a province complicated the situation very greatly with respect to registration and deregistration of the very bonds that were mentioned and that, therefore, there should be only one in each province. In the province of Quebec, where very large business is transacted, it was suggested that there should be a transfer office at the city of Quebec as well as at the city of Montreal, and I recall all these discussions that took place. The banks, of course, would like to have one at every second door, but that is no reason why they should have one for their convenience and why this Dominion should go to the expense of establishing a second receiver general's office in any one province. If my hon. friend will pardon me I will take him through a transaction of this kind. The banks have a certain amount of legal tender which they carry and there are certain provisions with respect to the redemption of notes, but very few redemptions take place in outlying sections. All the banks do is to go to the receivers general's office when they require legal tender and they get it in bills of $500, $1,000, $10,000, $1 or $2; but, generally speaking, the banks carry them in their own treasury. Desirous as I am of assisting business, I cannot see how we are going to do that by going to the expense of establishing another receiver general's office. I think I know exactly why this is being done. It is for the purpose of giving a little

Electricity Inspection Act
more convenience for some people who are affected and not for the business community at all. As surely as you put it on the statute books, the next week you will be called upon to implement your promise and then you will have to have another building, a deputy of the receiver general and another staff; you will have to put your silver and gold in that office and you will then have two offices that will serve no greater purpose than one. If the minister will go down to the receiver general's office in the city of Montreal he will see exactly what I mean. I have no doubt he has followed these transactions himself from day to day. They are very simple.

It is no serious trouble to
do business in the city of Victoria. The whole province of British Columbia does business there; it is the capital of the province. If we listened to all these demands, probably we should have to establish four or five more capitals throughout the country. There is an excellent steamboat service with the island, with two lines of boats running every day, boats as fine as any afloat. The people are accustomed to do their business there, and it is no more trouble to carry on this business in Victoria than if you had branches established elsewhere. In addition, I am quite sure that the moment you create this precedent in British Columbia you will have numerous demands of the same kind from olher provinces.

Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend and revise the Electricity Inspection Act to bring it into conformity with the existing conditions in electricity, in regard to the commercial unit of supply, the units of electrical measure, inspection standards, the verification of meters, and other related matters, and to provide for the appointment of a director and such assistants as may be deemed necessary.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Will the minister explain this resolution?

During the past twenty years, as every member of the house knows, remarkable progress has been made in all electrical equipment, and the terms used in the Electricity Inspection Act of 1907 do not cover all the equipment in use to-day for the measurement of electricity. It is therefore proposed to revise the act. It is algo proposed to amend the sections relating to the officers, to bring them under the terms of the Civil Service Act.- It is proposed also to eliminate a number of sections that are considered to be beyond the power of the Dominion parliament, also to eliminate some sections that are obsolete. When we consider the bill section by section I am sure the house will realize that a good deal of the old bill is obsolete due to the rapid changes that have taken place' in all things electrical.
